profiles.name: Robert Griffin
profiles.excerpt: Robert Griffin was a dependable West Coast radio character actor whose surviving work crosses prestige anthology, westerns and detective drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Robert Griffin was one of the professional supporting actors who gave Hollywood radio its depth. Personal biography is less complete than his broadcast record, but the surviving credits place him firmly inside the West Coast repertory system that supplied weekly anthology, western and detective programs with experienced voices.

Griffin worked repeatedly on Lux Radio Theatre and later appeared on western and crime series including The Six Shooter, Roy Rogers, The Line Up and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar. His career is representative of actors whose names rarely appeared above the title but whose reliability made ambitious network drama possible.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Griffin, nine The Six Shooter appearances, eight Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar episodes, six Roy Rogers performances, five The Line Up appearances and additional work on Let George Do It, Richard Diamond, Private Detective and The Adventures of Philip Marlowe.

profiles.name: Victor Rodman
profiles.excerpt: Victor Rodman carried a screen career that began in the silent era into decades of radio character work, especially crime, police and anthology drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Victor Rodman was born Victor Rottman Jr. in Arkansas in 1892 and began appearing in films in the 1910s. His acting career therefore stretched from silent pictures into radio and television, giving him an exceptionally long professional perspective on changing forms of American entertainment.

Radio used Rodman extensively as a character actor. He appeared on programs including Lux Radio Theatre, Dragnet, This Is Your FBI, Suspense, The Whistler, Gunsmoke and Tales of the Texas Rangers. His mature voice and screen experience made him particularly useful for policemen, officials, suspects and other authority figures.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Rodman, 12 each on Dragnet and This Is Your FBI, five Let George Do It appearances, three The New Adventures of Nero Wolfe episodes and additional work on Barrie Craig, Encore Theater and Night Beat.

profiles.name: Charlotte Lawrence
profiles.excerpt: Charlotte Lawrence was a versatile West Coast radio actress whose surviving credits span detective, suspense and anthology drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Charlotte Lawrence belongs to the large professional radio repertory whose broadcast credits survive more fully than personal biography. Her work places her repeatedly in the Los Angeles dramatic community of the 1940s and 1950s, moving among crime series, suspense anthologies and literary adaptations.

Lawrence appeared on Broadway Is My Beat, Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, Escape, The Whistler and This Is Your FBI, among other programs. That range shows the central skill of the radio character actress: creating a convincing new identity quickly, often with only a handful of scenes and no visual shorthand.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Broadway Is My Beat performances credited to Lawrence, six Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances, five Escape episodes, four each on The Whistler and This Is Your FBI, and three each on CBS Radio Workshop, Lux Radio Theatre and The Adventures of Philip Marlowe.

profiles.name: Leo Cleary
profiles.excerpt: Leo Cleary was one of Lux Radio Theatre's essential stock players, the kind of supporting actor who helped weekly star vehicles sound fully inhabited.
profiles.bio_html:
Leo Cleary built a long career in Southern California entertainment before becoming a fixture in radio. He had stage and vaudeville experience and, by the network era, was established as a dependable Hollywood supporting actor with the flexibility to move quickly through small but necessary dramatic roles.

Lux Radio Theatre became the center of Cleary's radio career. Later recollections from people who worked around the program described him as a pillar of the Lux stock company, a revealing description of the professionals who surrounded each week's movie stars and made complicated one-hour adaptations possible on a live schedule.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 35 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Cleary, five Broadway Is My Beat appearances, three The Whistler episodes, two each on Jeff Regan, Investigator, Roy Rogers and The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show, plus additional work on Let George Do It and Tales of the Texas Rangers.

profiles.name: Lynn Allen
profiles.excerpt: Lynn Allen was a busy West Coast radio repertory actress whose surviving work is especially strong in western, literary and detective drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Lynn Allen is another radio professional whose surviving cast record says more than later biographical summaries. She worked regularly in the Hollywood dramatic companies of the 1950s, appearing in westerns, crime programs and prestige adaptations that depended on actors able to establish character almost immediately.

Her credits include repeated appearances on Have Gun, Will Travel, Gunsmoke, NBC University Theater and The Adventures of Philip Marlowe. In western drama especially, Allen could move among settlers, wives, victims and suspects while keeping each performance distinct within programs that reused the same supporting company.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 11 Have Gun, Will Travel performances credited to Allen, ten each on Gunsmoke and NBC University Theater, eight The Adventures of Philip Marlowe episodes, four each on Rocky Fortune and Screen Directors Playhouse, and additional work on Fort Laramie and Barrie Craig.

profiles.name: Frank Hemingway
profiles.excerpt: Frank Hemingway combined acting and narration with a long career as a network newscaster, becoming a familiar West Coast broadcast voice for decades.
profiles.bio_html:
Frank Hemingway entered broadcasting after earlier theatrical work and built a career that ranged from acting to news and commentary. He worked at stations in Oregon before moving into network broadcasting and became a prominent West Coast newscaster during the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s.

Hemingway also worked in dramatic and narrative radio. The Roy Rogers Show used him as narrator, placing his polished broadcast delivery inside one of radio's most popular western programs. His broader career as a newscaster and commentator makes announcing and narration a genuine second professional category rather than a minor credit.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 53 Roy Rogers performances credited to Hemingway. That concentrated holding captures the dramatic side of a broadcaster whose larger career was built around the authority and personality of his voice.

profiles.name: Ted Donaldson
profiles.excerpt: Ted Donaldson moved from child radio work and Broadway into films before returning to a major continuing radio role as Bud Anderson on Father Knows Best.
profiles.bio_html:
Ted Donaldson began acting as a child in the late 1930s, first appearing on radio before moving into Broadway and film. He played Harlan in the stage production of Life with Father and later became a familiar juvenile screen actor in films including A Tree Grows in Brooklyn and the Rusty series.

Radio remained an important part of Donaldson's career. From 1949 to 1954 he played Bud Anderson, the teenage son of Robert Young's Jim Anderson, on the NBC version of Father Knows Best. The role placed him in one of radio's most influential family comedies and required the timing of a continuing ensemble rather than the one-off work common to child actors.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 52 Father Knows Best performances credited to Donaldson and one The Railroad Hour appearance. Those broadcasts preserve the role that became the center of his radio career after his earlier child-performer years.

profiles.name: Bert Holland
profiles.excerpt: Bert Holland combined a substantial radio acting career with directing, producing and teaching, carrying professional studio experience into educational theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Bertram "Bert" Holland was born in 1922 and built a career across theater, radio, television and motion pictures. His papers preserve scripts from major radio programs as well as commercials and theatrical productions, reflecting a working life that extended beyond performance alone.

Holland later produced numerous plays and taught at Santa Monica College, where he became head of the Theater Arts Department. He was also active in AFTRA and the Screen Actors Guild. That directing and producing work is retained as a genuine second professional category alongside the radio acting heard in detective, western and anthology programs.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 23 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Holland, six The Six Shooter appearances, five Tales of the Texas Rangers episodes, four The Adventures of Frank Race performances, three Broadway Is My Beat appearances and additional work on The Adventures of Philip Marlowe, The Line Up and CBS Radio Workshop.

profiles.name: Jean Vander Pyl
profiles.excerpt: Jean Vander Pyl built a long radio career before becoming one of animation's most recognizable voices as Wilma Flintstone.
profiles.bio_html:
Jean Vander Pyl was born in Philadelphia in 1919 and began working in radio after graduating from Beverly Hills High School. She became a versatile Hollywood microphone actress, handling roles that ranged from ingenues to older women and developing the voice control that later made her an important animation performer.

On radio, Vander Pyl played Margaret Anderson on Father Knows Best and worked on other comedy and dramatic programs. Her later career at Hanna-Barbera included Wilma Flintstone, Pebbles and numerous characters on The Jetsons and other animated series. That success grew directly from the anonymous but technically demanding radio work she had been doing for years.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 46 Father Knows Best performances credited to Vander Pyl, two each on Fibber McGee and Molly and Lux Radio Theatre, and additional appearances on The Halls of Ivy and Wild Bill Hickok.

profiles.name: Nigel Bruce
profiles.excerpt: Nigel Bruce made Dr. Watson one of radio's most familiar character voices, carrying his partnership with Basil Rathbone from film into The New Adventures of Sherlock Holmes.
profiles.bio_html:
Nigel Bruce was born in 1895 and built a distinguished British stage and screen career before Hollywood made him internationally familiar. His defining role became Dr. John Watson opposite Basil Rathbone's Sherlock Holmes, first in films and then on radio.

Bruce played Watson in more than two hundred broadcasts of The New Adventures of Sherlock Holmes. His interpretation emphasized warmth, loyalty and comic bewilderment, sometimes more broadly than Arthur Conan Doyle's original character, but the chemistry between Bruce and Rathbone became one of the most durable Holmes pairings of the twentieth century.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 48 The New Adventures of Sherlock Holmes performances credited to Bruce and two Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts. Those holdings document the radio side of the role that became inseparable from his public identity.
